opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it is this: internet AI, the large language models we've all been amazed by, learned from what humans have already written down. It's a kind of intelligence distilled from text, images, and videos on the web. It's extraordinary, but it lives in a world of symbols. It can tell you how to fold a shirt, but it has never felt the fabric slip between its fingers.

Embodied intelligence asks a different question. Can an intelligent system perceive the physical world, make decisions in real time, and act through a body to change that world? That's a much harder problem, because the physical world doesn't forgive you. If a language model makes a mistake, you regenerate the answer. If a robot misjudges the friction on a cup, the cup falls and breaks.

So the ambition, as I see it, is to close the loop between perception, cognition, and action. Intelligence in nature was never separated from the body. A child learns what "heavy" means by lifting things, and learns what "fragile" means by breaking things. We believe that for AI to truly understand the world, and to be truly useful to people, it has to go through a similar process of interacting with the world.

There's also a very practical side. Most of the value in the economy, things like manufacturing, logistics, household chores, and elderly care, happens in the physical world. Internet AI has transformed information work, but a huge share of human labor is still physical. If we can build general-purpose robots that can handle open-ended tasks, not just repeat one motion on an assembly line, that would be a transformation on the scale of the industrial revolution.

The biggest bottleneck, in my view, is data. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. For robots there's no internet of actions. Nobody has uploaded billions of hours of joint torques and tactile feedback. So a lot of our work is about how to get there, combining large-scale synthetic data from simulation with real-world data, so that a model can learn general skills and then transfer them to real robots. Once we solve the data problem, I believe embodied intelligence could follow a scaling path similar to what we saw with large language models.

So it's not just moving AI from screens into machines. It's about letting intelligence finally touch the world.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied intelligence perceives the physical world, but does not present selecting what to observe as an aim.

r002.rationale: It describes making decisions and acting through a body to change the world, communicating the aim of choosing how to affect what is observed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the ambition is not new. If you go back to the very beginning of artificial intelligence, the dream was never a chatbot. The dream was a machine that could perceive the world, reason about it, and act in it. A robot, basically. The internet era just gave us a very convenient detour.

What happened over the last ten years is that the internet accumulated an enormous amount of human knowledge in text and images, and we discovered that if you compress that knowledge into a large model, you get something that looks very much like general intelligence. Language, coding, math, images. But notice what all of that has in common. It lives entirely inside a computer. The model reads bits and produces bits. It never has to deal with gravity, friction, a cup that is slightly wet, a door that sticks a little. Nothing it does has physical consequences.

So the way I understand this transition is that internet AI solved the problem of the brain in a jar. We now have a very capable brain, and it is sitting in a jar. Embodied intelligence is about taking it out of the jar and connecting it to a body that has to survive and accomplish things in the real physical world. That is a qualitatively different problem, and I think a lot of people underestimate how different it is.

There are a few reasons why it is so different. The first is data. The internet gave us trillions of tokens of text for free, because humans spent decades writing things down. There is no equivalent for robot actions. Nobody has recorded, at scale, how a hand closes around a bottle, what forces it feels, how it adjusts when the bottle is heavier than expected. That data does not exist on the internet. We have to generate it, either by collecting it in the real world, which is slow and expensive, or by building simulations good enough that the data transfers to reality. A lot of my own research has been betting on the second path, because I think it is the only way to reach internet scale.

The second is that in the physical world, you cannot pause. A language model can think for ten seconds before answering. A robot carrying a tray cannot. Perception, decision, and control have to be happening continuously, in a closed loop, and mistakes are not just wrong answers, they can break something or hurt someone. So the bar for reliability is completely different. Ninety percent is impressive for a benchmark. Ninety percent is unacceptable for a robot in a pharmacy or a home.

The third thing, and this is the part I find genuinely exciting, is that a body changes what intelligence even means. A lot of what we call common sense is actually physical intuition that we learned as infants by grabbing things, dropping things, bumping into things. Language models inherit a shadow of that through text, but it is secondhand. When you give a model a body and let it interact with the world, it gets access to a kind of knowledge that no amount of reading can provide. So I do not see embodied AI as just an application of large models. I see it as the next source of intelligence itself.

As for the word ambition, I would put it this way. If large language models are about digitizing human knowledge, embodied intelligence is about digitizing human labor. That is a much larger piece of the economy and a much larger piece of what it means to be useful in the world. The internet changed how we exchange information. Robots that can actually do things will change how we produce and live. That is the scale of what we are trying to do, and it is why I left pure research and started building a company around it. You cannot do this from inside a paper. You have to put the robot in the real world and let the real world teach you where you are wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes perceiving the world and interacting with it, but does not present choosing what to observe as an aim of embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response says embodied intelligence acts in the physical world, but does not present choosing how to change what it observes as an aim.

astra-6.text:
I think the ambition is to move from understanding and describing the world to being able to act in it. On the internet, an AI can produce an answer, and that answer can be useful on its own. When intelligence controls a body, it has to close the loop: perceive what is happening, decide what to do, act, and then observe whether the action had the intended effect.

Even something as simple as picking up a cup brings all of that together. Where should you grasp it? How much force should you use? What happens if it slips? You cannot solve the task just by knowing how to explain it. You have to keep responding to the physical world.

So the ambition is larger than giving a chatbot arms and legs. It is to build intelligence that can turn an intention into a reliable physical outcome. And that raises a fundamental question: how much of intelligence comes from learning through interaction, through seeing the consequences of your own actions? A body gives us a way to explore that.

r001.rationale: The response mentions perceiving and observing outcomes, but does not present choosing what to observe as an aim of embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response describes choosing and taking physical actions, but does not clearly frame their aim as choosing how to change what the system observes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the ambition is to move from understanding and generating information to actually getting things done in the physical world. Internet AI mostly interacts through text, images, and video. An embodied system has to perceive its surroundings, decide what to do, act, and then adjust based on what happens.

That feedback loop changes the problem. If a robot picks up a cup, recognizing the cup is only part of the task. It also needs to work out how to grasp it, how much force to apply, and what to do if it starts slipping. Its understanding has to support action under uncertainty.

So the ambition is broader than giving a chatbot a body. It is to build intelligence that can learn through interaction and reliably turn an intention into a physical outcome. That could make AI useful in many more parts of everyday life, but it also sets a much higher bar for reliability.

r001.rationale: It says embodied AI perceives its surroundings and adjusts based on what happens, but does not present choosing what to observe as an aim.

r002.rationale: It describes acting on the physical world, such as grasping a cup, but does not present choosing how to change what it observes as an aim.
